correctness.rationale: For any edge subset of a tree, forbidding three marked edges on a simple path is exactly bounding the induced 0/1 weighted diameter by two. At a child-to-parent attachment, the new branch height is \(h=a+b\) for child height a and incident-edge choice b. When two different branches meet at v, their worst joining path has marked weight equal to the sum of their respective maximum root heights; thus the compatibility criterion \(a+h\le 2\) is necessary and sufficient. The maximum state updates by \(\max\{a,h\}\). Induction proves the recurrence without omission or double counting. Dense coefficient convolution across rooted child merges uses at most \(O(n^2)\) integer arithmetic operations. Independently enumerated paths tested 18,744 labeled-tree cases and 1,390,623 masks; 100 double-stars and 120 path/star boundary formulas also matched. Finite tests are not substituted for the proof.

originality.rationale: Compared implication-level content against the accessible 2021 foundational tree maximum theorem, the full relevant HTML content of 2023 partial-cube and 2024 extremal/block-graph papers, a published spider-family count, and related earlier mathematical claims. The maximum equals the number of leaves but does not determine the full coefficient distribution; the spider formula applies only to trees with at most one branching vertex; the other works concern extremal sets or other classes. The present theorem is an all-tree \(O(n^2)\) full cardinality algorithm with a branch-merge invariant. Searches found no covering statement, while incomplete index coverage and an unretrieved spider full record remain risks.

value.rationale: Published extremal edge-GP numbers tell only the largest feasible size; a complete distribution is a separate natural invariant that otherwise involves up to \(2^{n-1}\) subsets. The result supplies an exact polynomial-time coefficient algorithm on every tree, independent of branch-count or topology, with an explicit three-state criterion and provable quadratic arithmetic bound. Spider-tree formulas do not handle the interaction between several branching vertices, which is handled by the merge rule. The theorem is substantially more than a minor numeric increment; the double-star calculation provides an illustrative non-spider application.
